paras: The lynching of Jim Saunders was the shooting of an eighteen-year-old Black youth by masked men in Union township, Arkansas, about ten to twelve miles from Little Rock, on the night of Sunday, May 28, 1882. Saunders, accused of attempting to assault a white girl, was being held under a constable's guard when the men overpowered the guards and riddled him with bullets. The killing was carried by wire across the country, and local papers reported anger among Black residents and fears of further violence.

According to the Little Rock Democrat, Nannie Carr, the ward of R. S. Parker, went to Parker's schoolhouse on Saturday evening, May 27, to prepare it for Sunday services. The Democrat said that Saunders crept into the building and seized her from behind, and that he fled when a man named Wm. Pinson came to the window and fired at him. A Times-Democrat special gave a different version, in which Saunders arrived with a gun, asked for a drink, and then seized and choked her before escaping through a window. Both versions came from the accusers' side, and no account from Saunders appears.

Saunders made his way to Little Rock, where Chief of Police Counts arrested him at Main and Eighth streets on Sunday afternoon. Counts turned him over to Deputy Constable Carter Walls and a posse, who took him to Union and delivered him to Magistrate McAllister, who placed him in the charge of Constable Monroe Bowen. He was held in a small house near the mill, described elsewhere as a frame building, to await a hearing.

That night a 'large body of masked men' broke into the building, overpowered the guards and shot Saunders dead where he was held. The Democrat put the time at 10 o'clock, while the Times-Democrat and a Chicago-relayed special said about midnight.

Deputy Sheriff Botsford and Coroner Woolford left Little Rock for the scene the next morning, and the coroner held an inquest that day. No verdict of the inquest appears in the coverage, though one report said threats of further trouble were made while it sat. The Ottawa Free Trader reported that some of the masked men were said to have been recognized and would likely be indicted, but no report of an indictment or trial was found.

Magistrate McAllister told a reporter he feared a collision between whites and Blacks, and dispatches described the Black residents of the neighborhood as 'greatly excited and incensed' and 'very bitter.' On the following Sunday, according to the Little Rock Gazette, white families near Wrightsville and Sweet Home hid in the woods on a rumor that Black residents were arming, while Black residents heard that their church had been fired into and two people murdered. The sheriff investigated and found the whole a groundless scare.

Coverage came only from the white press, starting on May 30 with a Little Rock wire that the Savannah Morning News ran as 'Riddled with Bullets.' Shorter versions of the same wire appeared in Sacramento, Salt Lake City, Unionville, Nevada, Bel Air, Maryland, and Jackson, Mississippi, over the next week. The Memphis Public Ledger reprinted the Little Rock Democrat's fuller local account under 'Swift Retribution,' and the Brookhaven Ledger carried the Times-Democrat special under a headline saying Saunders 'is Lynched by a Mob.'

Headlines such as 'A Negro Ravisher Shot' in Yankton and 'Summary Vengeance' in Ottawa, Illinois, treated the accusation as proven, and the Yankton dispatch called Saunders 'guilty' though he had not been tried. The Little Rock Gazette, a week later, described the killing more plainly as a shooting 'while in the hands of officers of the law' and gave most of its attention to the scare that followed.

Accounts differed on minor points: the girl was 'Nannie Corrie' in one dispatch, the building was called a small house, a frame building, a calaboose or a jail, and the distance from Little Rock was given as ten or twelve miles.

bases: A body of masked men broke into the building where a constable's guard held Saunders, overpowered the guards and shot him dead (A1, A2, A8).

Saunders was shot dead by a 'large body' of masked men who took him from the guards of a constable while he awaited a hearing on a charge of attempted assault on a white girl (A1, A2, A8, A10); the Times-Democrat headline called it lynching 'by a Mob' (A8).

The Little Rock Democrat (A1), a Little Rock wire (A2), a Times-Democrat special (A8) and a Chicago-relayed special (A3) agree on the arrest, the guarded building and the shooting by masked men, and the Little Rock Gazette later confirmed the killing (A12).
